questions.title: Ureter crosses the obturator nerve and vessels in the pelvis
questions.question: In the pelvis, the ureter crosses which of the following structures as it descends toward the bladder along the lateral pelvic wall?

explanations.A: Correct. As the ureter descends into the pelvis it runs on the medial aspect of the internal iliac vessels and crosses anterior to the obturator nerve and vessels near the lateral pelvic wall, at the point where these structures enter the obturator canal. This obturator crossing is the classic surgical landmark cited when identifying the ureter during pelvic surgery, since the ureter must be traced across this point to avoid inadvertent ligation. The uterine artery in females later crosses anterior to the ureter more medially ('water under the bridge'), but that is a separate, more distal relation from the obturator crossing being tested here.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The inferior epigastric vessels arise from the external iliac vessels and run superiorly in the anterior abdominal wall; the ureter does not cross them as it descends in the pelvis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The lumbosacral trunk lies posterior on the pelvic side wall and is not the structure the ureter is described as crossing on its pelvic course.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The internal pudendal nerve leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen and re-enters via the lesser sciatic foramen to reach the perineum; it is not the neurovascular bundle the ureter crosses in the pelvic wall.

questions.subject: renal
questions.learning_objective: Identify the obturator nerve and vessels as the structures the ureter crosses in the lesser pelvis.

questions.title: Right kidney posterior relations spare the 11th rib
questions.question: The right kidney is related posteriorly to all of the following EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Correct. The right kidney sits slightly lower than the left because of the liver above it, so posteriorly it is related to only the 12th rib, not the 11th rib; the left kidney, which sits higher, is related to both the 11th and 12th ribs posteriorly. This asymmetry is a classic exam point distinguishing the two kidneys' rib relations. The 11th rib is therefore the correct answer to this 'except' question, since it is the one listed structure that is NOT actually a posterior relation of the right kidney.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The 12th rib IS a posterior relation of the right kidney (crossing its upper pole), so it does not answer an 'except' question about relations that are absent.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The diaphragm IS a posterior relation of the upper pole of the right kidney, so it does not answer an 'except' question about relations that are absent.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Psoas major IS a posterior relation of the right kidney medially, so it does not answer an 'except' question about relations that are absent.

questions.subject: renal
questions.learning_objective: Distinguish the right kidney's posterior rib relations (12th rib only) from the left kidney's (11th and 12th ribs).

questions.title: Conivaptan is contraindicated in hypovolemic hyponatremia
questions.question: Regarding the management of SIADH, which of the following statements about conivaptan is true?

options.A: It is contraindicated in hypovolemic hyponatremia
options.B: It is a loop diuretic used first-line in SIADH
options.C: It is safe and preferred in hypovolemic hyponatremia
options.D: It works by directly inhibiting aquaporin-2 gene synthesis

explanations.A: Correct. Conivaptan is a non-selective vasopressin V1A/V2-receptor antagonist ('vaptan') used to treat euvolemic or hypervolemic hyponatremia, including SIADH; because it promotes free-water excretion (aquaresis) without retaining sodium, it is contraindicated in hypovolemic hyponatremia, where it would worsen intravascular volume depletion. Vaptans are reserved for states of water excess, not volume depletion, and using one in a hypovolemic patient can precipitate or worsen hypotension. This distinction — euvolemic/hypervolemic hyponatremia versus hypovolemic hyponatremia — determines whether a vaptan is an appropriate treatment.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Conivaptan is not a loop diuretic; it is a vasopressin-receptor antagonist that causes aquaresis (free-water excretion) rather than natriuresis, and loop diuretics are not first-line therapy for SIADH.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Conivaptan is specifically contraindicated, not preferred, in hypovolemic hyponatremia because it would further reduce effective circulating volume.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Conivaptan acts by blocking vasopressin V2 receptors in the collecting duct, which secondarily reduces aquaporin-2 trafficking to the luminal membrane; it does not directly inhibit aquaporin-2 gene synthesis.

questions.subject: pharm
questions.learning_objective: State that conivaptan (a vasopressin-receptor antagonist) is contraindicated in hypovolemic hyponatremia.

questions.title: Glycine is a purely glucogenic amino acid
questions.question: Which of the following amino acids is classified as purely glucogenic?

explanations.A: Correct. Amino acids are classified by their metabolic fate into pure glucogenic, pure ketogenic, or mixed groups; glycine, like most amino acids, is degraded to intermediates (via serine, then pyruvate) that can feed gluconeogenesis, making it purely glucogenic. Only two amino acids, leucine and lysine, are purely ketogenic, and only four (phenylalanine, tyrosine, tryptophan and isoleucine) are mixed glucogenic-and-ketogenic. Every other amino acid, including glycine, is purely glucogenic.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Leucine is one of only two amino acids (with lysine) that is purely ketogenic, not glucogenic — it is degraded entirely to acetyl-CoA/acetoacetate with no net carbon entering gluconeogenesis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Lysine, like leucine, is purely ketogenic, not glucogenic.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Isoleucine is one of the four amino acids classified as glucogenic-and-ketogenic (mixed), not purely glucogenic.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Classify glycine as a purely glucogenic amino acid, distinct from the purely ketogenic (leucine, lysine) and mixed (phenylalanine, tyrosine, tryptophan, isoleucine) groups.

questions.title: Carnitine deficiency causes muscle weakness and fasting hypoglycemia
questions.question: A patient presents with proximal muscle weakness and episodes of hypoglycemia during fasting. Which of the following metabolic defects best explains this presentation?

explanations.A: Correct. Carnitine is required to shuttle long-chain fatty acyl groups across the inner mitochondrial membrane for beta-oxidation; carnitine deficiency impairs fatty-acid oxidation, so muscle cannot use fat for energy and the liver cannot support ketogenesis and gluconeogenesis as efficiently during fasting, producing proximal muscle weakness together with fasting hypoglycemia. This combination — muscle weakness plus fasting hypoglycemia with low ketones (hypoketotic hypoglycemia) — is the classic presentation of a fatty-acid oxidation defect such as carnitine deficiency. Skeletal and cardiac muscle are especially affected because they rely heavily on fatty-acid oxidation for energy.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency (von Gierke disease) causes fasting hypoglycemia through impaired glycogenolysis/gluconeogenesis output, but its hallmark is severe hepatomegaly with lactic acidosis, hyperuricemia and hyperlipidemia, not primarily proximal muscle weakness from a fat-oxidation defect.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Pyruvate kinase deficiency causes a hereditary hemolytic anemia from a red-cell glycolytic defect, not muscle weakness with fasting hypoglycemia.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency causes early-onset emphysema and liver disease, not a muscle-weakness/fasting-hypoglycemia syndrome.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Recognize carnitine deficiency as a fatty-acid oxidation defect presenting with muscle weakness and fasting hypoglycemia.

questions.title: 21-alpha-hydroxylase deficiency causes precocious puberty
questions.question: A defect in the enzyme 21-alpha-hydroxylase is most likely to result in which of the following?

options.B: Delayed puberty with low androgen levels

explanations.A: Correct. 21-alpha-hydroxylase deficiency (the most common cause of congenital adrenal hyperplasia) blocks the synthesis of cortisol and aldosterone from their shared precursor, 17-hydroxyprogesterone; the resulting precursor buildup is shunted into the androgen synthesis pathway, causing excess adrenal androgen production. In either sex the chronic androgen excess drives early (precocious) puberty and accelerated but ultimately compromised growth. This is a distinct clinical facet of the same enzyme defect from the salt-wasting, hyponatremic crisis caused by the accompanying aldosterone deficiency.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 21-alpha-hydroxylase deficiency causes androgen excess, not deficiency, so it produces early puberty with high, not low, androgen levels.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 21-alpha-hydroxylase acts in adrenal steroidogenesis, not the growth hormone axis, and does not cause isolated growth hormone deficiency.
explanations.D: Incorrect. 21-alpha-hydroxylase deficiency affects adrenal cortisol/aldosterone/androgen synthesis, not thyroid hormone synthesis, and does not cause primary hypothyroidism.

questions.subject: renal
questions.learning_objective: State that 21-alpha-hydroxylase deficiency causes precocious puberty via adrenal androgen excess, alongside its separately-tested salt-wasting hyponatremia.

questions.title: Renal glutaminase drives ammoniagenesis for acid-base balance
questions.question: Which of the following best describes the function of renal glutaminase?

options.A: It deaminates glutamine to generate ammonia for renal acid-base balance
options.B: It converts glucose to glutamine in the proximal tubule
options.C: It reabsorbs filtered bicarbonate in the loop of Henle
options.D: It is the rate-limiting enzyme of the hepatic urea cycle

explanations.A: Correct. Renal glutaminase, located mainly in proximal tubular cell mitochondria, deaminates glutamine to glutamate and ammonia (NH3); the ammonia is secreted into the tubular lumen where it combines with H+ to form ammonium (NH4+), which is excreted, allowing the kidney to excrete acid as ammonium while generating new bicarbonate that is returned to the blood. This ammoniagenesis pathway is upregulated during chronic acidosis and is one of the kidney's principal mechanisms — alongside titratable acid excretion — for maintaining acid-base balance. Without adequate glutaminase activity, the kidney's capacity to excrete a chronic acid load is impaired.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Glutaminase breaks glutamine down (to glutamate and ammonia); it does not synthesize glutamine from glucose.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Bicarbonate reabsorption occurs mainly via the sodium-hydrogen exchanger and carbonic anhydrase in the proximal tubule, not via glutaminase, and this process is distinct from ammoniagenesis.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Glutaminase is a renal (and hepatic) mitochondrial enzyme involved in acid-base handling and nitrogen metabolism, not the rate-limiting enzyme of the hepatic urea cycle (which is carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I).

questions.subject: renal
questions.learning_objective: Explain that renal glutaminase drives ammoniagenesis, a principal mechanism of renal acid-base balance.

questions.title: Homocystinuria weakens the extracellular matrix via defective lysine cross-linking
questions.question: In homocystinuria, weakening of the extracellular matrix is best explained by which of the following mechanisms?

options.A: Excess homocysteine disrupts normal lysine-dependent cross-linking of collagen
options.B: Excess homocysteine directly degrades elastin via elastase activation
options.C: Excess homocysteine impairs hydroxyproline formation in collagen
options.D: Excess homocysteine increases collagen cross-linking, causing tissue stiffness

explanations.A: Correct. In homocystinuria (most commonly from cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency), accumulated homocysteine reacts with the lysine residues that normally participate in the lysyl-oxidase-mediated cross-linking of collagen and elastin, disrupting normal cross-link formation. This produces a structurally weaker extracellular matrix, which underlies the classic features of homocystinuria — lens dislocation (ectopia lentis), skeletal changes resembling Marfan syndrome, and vascular fragility contributing to thromboembolism. The mechanism is therefore an interference with normal cross-linking chemistry rather than a change in collagen synthesis rate.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Homocystinuria's connective tissue weakness comes from disrupted lysine-dependent cross-linking, not from elastase-mediated degradation of elastin.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Hydroxyproline formation (via prolyl hydroxylase, which requires vitamin C) is the defect in scurvy, not the mechanism of connective tissue weakness in homocystinuria.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Homocysteine impairs, rather than increases, normal collagen cross-linking; increased cross-linking would make tissue stiffer, not weaker, which is the opposite of what is seen.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Explain that homocystinuria weakens the extracellular matrix by disrupting lysine-dependent collagen/elastin cross-linking.

questions.title: Intraglomerular mesangial cells perform basement membrane turnover
questions.question: Which of the following is a recognized function of the intraglomerular mesangial cells?

options.C: Renin secretion in response to reduced perfusion
options.D: Active tubular secretion of organic anions

explanations.A: Correct. Intraglomerular mesangial cells are modified smooth-muscle-like cells that sit between glomerular capillary loops; among their recognized functions is phagocytosis and turnover (synthesis and degradation) of the glomerular basement membrane and trapped macromolecules/immune complexes. They also provide structural support for the capillary tuft and, through their contractile properties, help regulate glomerular capillary surface area and filtration. This turnover function is distinct from the roles of other juxtaglomerular apparatus components.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Erythropoietin is produced by renal peritubular interstitial fibroblasts in the cortex and outer medulla, not by intraglomerular mesangial cells.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Renin is secreted by the granular (juxtaglomerular) cells of the afferent arteriole, a separate cell population from the intraglomerular mesangial cells, though both are part of the broader juxtaglomerular apparatus.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Active tubular secretion of organic anions occurs in proximal tubular epithelial cells, not in the mesangial cells of the glomerulus.

questions.subject: renal
questions.learning_objective: Identify basement membrane turnover as a recognized function of intraglomerular mesangial cells.

questions.title: Atrial natriuretic peptide compensates for IV-saline-induced overhydration
questions.question: A patient treated with excessive intravenous saline infusions becomes overhydrated. Which of the following is the expected compensatory response?

explanations.A: Correct. Volume overload from IV saline stretches the cardiac atria, which stimulates release of atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP); ANP promotes natriuresis and diuresis by increasing glomerular filtration rate, inhibiting sodium reabsorption in the collecting duct, and suppressing renin and aldosterone release, all of which act to excrete the excess volume and restore normal circulating volume. This is the physiological counter-regulatory response to hypervolemia, opposite in direction to the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system's response to hypovolemia. ANP is therefore the expected compensation in an overhydrated, volume-expanded state.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Aldosterone promotes sodium and water retention and would worsen, not compensate for, overhydration; its secretion is suppressed, not increased, in volume overload.
explanations.C: Incorrect. ADH promotes water retention and would worsen overhydration; volume expansion suppresses, rather than stimulates, ADH release (via low-pressure baroreceptor input).
explanations.D: Incorrect. Renin release is suppressed by volume expansion (via increased renal perfusion pressure and reduced sympathetic tone), not increased.

questions.subject: renal
questions.learning_objective: Identify ANP release, driven by atrial stretch, as the compensatory response to IV-saline-induced hypervolemia.

questions.title: The inner medullary collecting duct reabsorbs only a small fraction of filtered water
questions.question: Which of the following statements regarding renal water reabsorption is true?

options.A: Approximately 4.2% of filtered water is reabsorbed in the inner medullary collecting duct
options.B: Approximately 65% of filtered water is reabsorbed in the inner medullary collecting duct
options.C: No water is reabsorbed in the inner medullary collecting duct under any condition
options.D: Water reabsorption in the inner medullary collecting duct is independent of antidiuretic hormone

explanations.A: Correct. Along the nephron, most filtered water (roughly 65%) is reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule, with further reabsorption in the descending thin limb of the loop of Henle; only a small fraction remains to be handled by the distal nephron. Under antidiuretic hormone's influence, only a small percentage of the original filtrate — on the order of a few percent, cited here as approximately 4.2% — is reabsorbed in the inner medullary collecting duct, the final and most tightly regulated site of water reabsorption. This last segment is where the kidney fine-tunes urine concentration to match the body's hydration state.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Approximately 65% of filtered water is reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule, not the inner medullary collecting duct, which reabsorbs only a small residual fraction.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The inner medullary collecting duct does reabsorb water, particularly when antidiuretic hormone is present and aquaporin-2 channels are inserted into the luminal membrane.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Water reabsorption in the inner medullary collecting duct is critically dependent on antidiuretic hormone, which controls aquaporin-2 channel insertion; without ADH, this segment remains relatively water-impermeable.

questions.subject: renal
questions.learning_objective: State that only a small fraction (~4.2%) of filtered water is reabsorbed in the inner medullary collecting duct, the site of ADH-dependent fine urine concentration.

questions.title: Upper motor neuron lesion causes loss of voluntary control over micturition
questions.question: Regarding abnormal micturition following a suprasacral spinal cord lesion (upper motor neuron lesion), which of the following best describes the resulting change?

options.A: Loss of voluntary control over micturition, with an involuntary reflex bladder
options.B: Complete loss of the micturition reflex with painless bladder distension
options.C: Increased voluntary control with reduced reflex bladder contractions
options.D: Selective loss of bladder sensation with preserved voluntary voiding

explanations.A: Correct. A lesion above the sacral micturition center (an upper motor neuron lesion) disconnects the pontine and cortical centers that normally allow voluntary initiation and inhibition of voiding from the intact sacral reflex arc; the result is loss of voluntary control over micturition while the basic spinal detrusor reflex persists (and is often exaggerated), producing an involuntary 'reflex' or 'automatic' bladder with reflex incontinence. This contrasts with a lower motor neuron (sacral) lesion, which abolishes the reflex arc itself and produces an atonic, overflow-type bladder. The distinction between upper and lower motor neuron patterns of bladder dysfunction is a standard physiology and clinical teaching point.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Complete loss of the micturition reflex with painless bladder distension describes a lower motor neuron (sacral/infrasacral) lesion, which destroys the reflex arc itself, not a suprasacral upper motor neuron lesion, which spares and often exaggerates the reflex.
explanations.C: Incorrect. An upper motor neuron lesion above the sacral center reduces, not increases, voluntary control over micturition.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The characteristic upper motor neuron pattern is loss of voluntary control with a preserved/exaggerated reflex, not an isolated sensory deficit with preserved voluntary voiding.

questions.subject: renal
questions.learning_objective: Describe the upper motor neuron (suprasacral) pattern of abnormal micturition: loss of voluntary control with a preserved reflex bladder.

questions.title: Acidosis increases cellular potassium efflux and decreases renal potassium secretion
questions.question: In acidosis, which of the following best describes the effect on potassium handling?

options.A: Increased efflux of potassium out of cells and decreased renal potassium secretion
options.B: Decreased efflux of potassium out of cells and increased renal potassium secretion
options.C: No effect on cellular potassium efflux, but increased renal potassium secretion
options.D: Increased efflux of potassium out of cells and increased renal potassium secretion

explanations.A: Correct. In acidosis, excess extracellular hydrogen ions are buffered partly by movement into cells in exchange for intracellular potassium moving out, so cellular potassium efflux increases; at the same time, acidosis reduces the activity of the basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase in the distal nephron's principal cells and lowers luminal potassium secretion, so renal potassium secretion decreases. Both effects combine to predispose to hyperkalemia in acidotic states, particularly metabolic (mineral) acidosis with an inorganic acid load. This is the classic explanation for why acidosis and hyperkalemia are frequently seen together.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Acidosis increases, not decreases, potassium efflux from cells (via the H+/K+ exchange mechanism), and decreases, not increases, renal potassium secretion.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Acidosis does affect cellular potassium efflux (increasing it via the H+/K+ exchange mechanism), and it decreases, rather than increases, renal potassium secretion.
explanations.D: Incorrect. While acidosis does increase cellular potassium efflux, it decreases, not increases, renal potassium secretion — both changes act in the same (hyperkalemia-promoting) direction, not opposite ones.

questions.subject: renal
questions.learning_objective: Explain that acidosis increases cellular potassium efflux and decreases renal potassium secretion, both predisposing to hyperkalemia.

questions.title: Lupus nephritis shows mesangial immune complex deposits
questions.question: A patient with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) undergoes renal biopsy. Which of the following microscopic findings is characteristic of lupus nephritis?

options.B: Linear basement membrane deposits of anti-GBM antibody
options.C: Crescents composed purely of neutrophils with no immune deposits
options.D: Amyloid deposits staining positive with Congo red

explanations.A: Correct. Lupus nephritis is an immune-complex-mediated glomerulonephritis in which circulating immune complexes (often containing anti-dsDNA antibodies) deposit in the mesangium, and — depending on the class of lupus nephritis — also in the subendothelial and/or subepithelial regions of the glomerular basement membrane. Mesangial deposits are a defining light-microscopic and immunofluorescence finding across the spectrum of lupus nephritis classes, often producing a 'full-house' immunofluorescence pattern (IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, C1q). This immune-complex mechanism distinguishes lupus nephritis from other glomerular diseases with different deposit patterns.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Linear basement membrane deposits are characteristic of anti-glomerular basement membrane (anti-GBM) disease (e.g. Goodpasture syndrome), which reflects antibody binding directly to a basement membrane antigen, not the granular immune-complex deposition pattern of lupus nephritis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Crescents in glomerulonephritis are composed mainly of proliferating parietal epithelial cells and macrophages, not purely neutrophils, and lupus nephritis crescents occur alongside immune complex deposits rather than in their absence.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Amyloid deposits staining with Congo red are characteristic of renal amyloidosis, a different disease process from the immune-complex-mediated injury of lupus nephritis.

questions.subject: renal
questions.learning_objective: Identify mesangial immune complex deposits as the characteristic light-microscopic finding in lupus nephritis.
